Article Title: BJP's third-term bid, Congress's comeback hopes: What will decide Uttarakhand elections 2027?
Article Text:
BJP's hat-trick bid, Congress's comeback challenge: What is at stake in Uttarakhand (AI-generated image)

BJP has a historic second but can it pull off a third?

File photo: CM Dhami hails PM Modi's leadership as Uttarakhand celebrates State Foundation Day

Congress wants a comeback. But can it get its house in order?

Issues Congress is likely to raise in its election campaign:

Ankita Bhandari murder case:

File photo: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi sits with the parents of Ankita Bhandari during a sit-in protest at India Gate in New Delhi

Jobs and recruitment:

Migration:

Land laws:

Regional and electoral arithmetic:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What the 2027 contest will turn on

The hills have eyes.And no one needs to remember that more than the parties aiming to win Uttarakhand’s upcoming elections next year.The Pushkar Singh Dhami-led BJP government, has on more than a few occasions proclaimed that they are set to aim for a historic ‘hat-trick’ in the ‘Devbhoomi’. At a recent event in Dehradun, Union home minister Amit Shah set an ambitious target of winning more than 65 of the state's 70 assembly seats. He said the BJP was determined to return to power for a third consecutive term and ensure that the "voice of Uttarakhand" reaches Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.But can the BJP script another first by securing a third consecutive term in a state where governments traditionally changed every five years? Or can the Congress capitalise on anti-incumbency against the Dhami government to wrest back power and add another state to its tally?The BJP enters the election contest on the back of a historic victory in 2022, when it won 47 of Uttarakhand's 70 assembly seats to secure a second consecutive term for the first time since the state's formation in 2000. However, the victory came with some caveats. The party's tally fell sharply from the 57 seats it had won in 2017, while the Congress improved its count from 11 to 19. Although the BJP retained a comfortable majority, both its seat tally and vote share declined. The Congress, meanwhile, made gains but failed to mount a serious challenge to the BJP's hold on power.That gap between retaining power and losing ground is central to the 2027 contest.The BJP aims to defend its record and create history while containing local discontent; the Congress will have to demonstrate that its criticism can translate into organisation, candidates and a coherent alternative.Uttarakhand is also a state where narrow margins have shaped constituency results, making it a state where local politics and national political sentiments both need to be paid heed to.For its first four elections, the state changed hands every time. Congress won 36 seats in 2002, the BJP 35 in 2007, Congress edged ahead 32 to 31 in 2012, and the BJP took 57 in 2017.The year 2022 proved to be historic for BJP as they became the first party to get a consecutive term in the state, even as their vote share slipped from 46.5 to 44.3 per cent while Congress rose from about 33.5 to nearly 38.The BJP enters 2027 legislative assembly elections wanting to retain the ‘Devbhoomi’, consistently highlighting their work within its boundaries and reiterating their claim of making it the cultural capital of the country.The party’s manifesto is sure to highlight: PM Narendra Modi’s national appeal, chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami ’s state-level leadership and the promise that having the same party in power at the Centre and in the state can accelerate development. The BJP is expected to make this double-engine argument a central part of its campaign, pointing to infrastructure projects, road connectivity, pilgrimage tourism and welfare schemes as evidence of what this political alignment can deliver.The party has already signalled that Dhami will remain its face in the 2027 election. National president Nitin Nabin indicated this during his May visit, while also stressing the need for a strategy tailored to Uttarakhand rather than one copied from other states. The leadership arrangement allows the BJP to combine the Prime Minister’s popularity with Dhami’s visibility as the head of the state government. It also gives the party a way to frame the election around continuity, arguing that another term would allow ongoing projects and policies to be carried forward.The party is also working to consolidate its social coalition across the state’s varied electorate. Uttarakhand’s political arithmetic includes upper-caste communities, particularly Brahmins and Rajputs, Scheduled Castes, OBC groups, and communities in the Terai and plains with distinct local and regional interests. The BJP’s challenge is to retain its existing support while expanding its appeal among groups where the Congress and other parties remain competitive. Its outreach to Dalit communities has acquired particular visibility amid the political dispute over the alleged purification ritual at Haldwani’s Ramlila Maidan after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s rally. Both parties have sought to engage Scheduled Caste voters in the aftermath of the controversy.Women and younger voters are also important to the party’s calculations. Reports on the BJP’s preparations suggest that it is considering additional welfare announcements aimed at women, alongside measures to address youth employment and migration. Its outreach has also included ex-servicemen and members of the Sikh community.The BJP’s development narrative is closely linked to its emphasis on religious identity and pilgrimage infrastructure. The Uniform Civil Code, implemented in January 2025, is among the Dhami government’s most prominent policy initiatives. The party has also highlighted the development of religious sites, expansion of tourism infrastructure and preparations for the Haridwar Kumbh.Organisation is set to be another pillar of their strategy, during his September visit to Haldwani, Nabin called on party workers to strengthen the booth-level network and work towards winning every booth. Their emphasis is not simply on mobilising workers closer to polling day, but on maintaining contact with voters, communicating government schemes and identifying constituencies where the party needs to improve its performance.The party is also considering a generational reset in its candidate selection. A TOI report said the BJP is weighing a greater emphasis on younger leaders and women, with performance, voter connect, public acceptance and organisational strength likely to determine ticket allocation. The party has conducted surveys to assess its sitting MLAs, and internal discussions suggest that 20-25% of them could lose their tickets if they receive poor feedback from their constituencies. State BJP president Mahendra Bhatt has maintained that winnability will be the key criterion.The BJP has also sought to make voter-list revision part of its political messaging around identity and demographic change. At a party meeting in Dehradun in June, state president Mahendra Bhatt urged workers to participate actively in the revision of electoral rolls and ensure that those the party described as “infiltrators” and other ineligible persons were removed. “Only the original people of Devbhoomi should decide the government," he said. The remarks reflect how the BJP is linking its appeal around Uttarakhand’s cultural identity with questions of who belongs in the state and who should shape its political future.Taken together, these moves show that the BJP is approaching 2027 with a campaign built around continuity, development, cultural identity and a tighter electoral organisation. But a third term will depend on whether these themes can hold up against the everyday concerns of voters. Questions of jobs, recruitment, migration, land rights and public services are unlikely to disappear simply because the party has sharpened its campaign machinery. For the BJP, the challenge is not only to make history, but to prevent local discontent from becoming a vote against it.The Congress did improve their performance in the 2022 elections but the reality is that they still lost. To make a comeback in the region, Congress will have to not only identify local discontent and areas of vulnerability, but also build a campaign that can carry those issues across the state and maintain coordination among leaders with competing political interests.The party has begun its organisational preparations. On November 2, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi met senior Uttarakhand leaders in New Delhi, including state unit chief Ganesh Godiyal, leader of the opposition Yashpal Arya and senior leaders Pritam Singh and Harak Singh Rawat. Congress general secretary (organisation) K C Venugopal and state in-charge Kumari Selja also attended the meeting, which focused on the party’s strategy for the 2027 assembly elections.The meeting was accompanied by a sharper attack on the BJP government. Kharge accused the state government of failing on law and order, women's safety and accountability, while Venugopal raised allegations of corruption, land grabs, environmental mismanagement and irregularities in recruitment examinations. The party also invoked the Ankita Bhandari case, which is sure to take centre stage in their rejection of the Centre.The murder of 19-year-old Ankita Bhandari in September 2022 remains one of the most politically sensitive issues in Uttarakhand. Bhandari, who worked as a receptionist at the Vanantra resort near Rishikesh, was murdered by resort owner Pulkit Arya and two employees. All three were convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in May 2025. But the convictions have not brought an end to the family’s campaign for answers about the alleged involvement of an influential person, referred to as a “VIP”, in the circumstances leading to her murder.The controversy has acquired a more direct political dimension because Ankita’s parents have publicly named BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam in their allegations. Gautam, who was appointed governor of Sikkim in October, has denied any involvement and initiated defamation proceedings against those accusing him. The family has demanded that his appointment be put on hold until the investigation into the alleged VIP angle is completed.The family’s protests have also brought the case back into the national political spotlight. On October 14, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra joined Ankita’s parents at a sit-in near India Gate, where the family was protesting against Gautam’s appointment. Hours later, Delhi Police detained the parents and several Congress leaders; they were released the following morning. On November 4, the parents staged another sit-in near Rajghat and were removed by police.For the Congress, the case has become a prominent part of its challenge to the BJP government on women's safety and accountability. For the ruling party, the continuing protests and the questions raised by Ankita’s family have kept an unresolved controversy in public view, even after the murder trial concluded. As the state approaches another election, the issue is no longer limited to the crime itself; it also concerns the credibility and progress of the investigation into the alleged VIP angle, the family's demand for answers and the government's response to their campaign.The cancellation of the Uttarakhand Subordinate Services Selection Commission’s graduate-level examination in September 2025, after a paper leak was confirmed at an examination centre in Haridwar, renewed questions about the credibility of the recruitment process. More than one lakh candidates had appeared for an examination for 416 posts, and the cancellation triggered protests. The episode also raised questions about the implementation of the state’s 2023 anti-cheating law, which had been introduced after earlier recruitment controversiesPeople leave remote hill villages not only for jobs, but also for better access to education, healthcare, transport and other basic services. The government has cited efforts to encourage reverse migration, but claims of improvement need to be measured against reliable data on village populations, employment and public services. The issue is not simply whether people are returning, but whether they can build sustainable lives in the hills.The 2025 amendment to Uttarakhand’s land laws restricted the purchase of agricultural and horticultural land by people from outside the state in 11 hill districts. While the government has presented this as a measure to protect local interests, campaigners argue that exemptions and the treatment of urban areas leave important gaps.The debate reflects a wider concern over local control of land and resources, and whether the aspirations behind Uttarakhand’s creation in 2000 have been fulfilled. Gairsain, designated as the summer capital, remains central to this discussion, particularly for those who believe development and administration have yet to reach remote hill regions.The Uttarakhand Kranti Dal (UKD), closely associated with the statehood movement, continues to represent some of these concerns. It had four MLAs in the first Assembly in 2002, but its representation declined sharply in subsequent elections. Its decision to field candidates in 2027 signals an attempt to reclaim the debate over regional identity and local rights, though its electoral influence remains limited.Uttarakhand's politics is shaped by differences between Garhwal and Kumaon, as well as the plains and Terai. The identities and local concerns of Garhwalis and Kumaonis form part of the state's political landscape, but they do not translate into fixed voting blocs. Employment, migration, land rights, infrastructure and access to public services can carry different weight across districts. The plains and Terai, meanwhile, have distinct demographic and economic dynamics. Congress will need to build a campaign that addresses these regional differences rather than assume that a single statewide message will resonate equally across all 70 constituencies.But the most dire step that Congress needs to take is to reconcile its senior leadership with the push for a more coordinated and visible state unit. The party can raise all the issues they want but unlike the BJP, they no longer have an established face to lead their campaigns. To put it lightly, their established faces have lost face during the previous elections.The BJP has already made Congress's internal differences part of its political argument. The Congress, in turn, is seeking to make governance and accountability the focus of the contest. Whether it can sustain that approach through a coordinated campaign, a stronger presence across constituencies and a clear leadership structure will be one of the defining questions of 2027.The BJP is seeking to make the election a referendum on continuity: its record in office, the leadership of Pushkar Singh Dhami, infrastructure development, welfare and the UCC.The Congress is trying to frame the election around accountability, employment, recruitment, migration, land and women’s safety.But the contest will ultimately be shaped by how voters across the state assess these competing claims. The BJP has the advantage of an established organisation and a second consecutive term behind it. The Congress has a list of grievances it hopes to turn into a campaign, but must still demonstrate that it can offer a coordinated alternative.The hills have eyes. They have watched governments come and go, and now they decide who they watch for the next 5 years.
Article Summary: BJP has a historic second but can it pull off a third? Congress wants a comeback. But can the Congress capitalise on anti-incumbency against the Dhami government to wrest back power and add another state to its tally? Uttarakhand is also a state where narrow margins have shaped constituency results.

NEW DELHI: Andhra Pradesh chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Monday renewed his call for withdrawing Rs 500 currency notes, arguing that limiting cash transactions to smaller denominations and encouraging digital payments could help curb corruption.Naidu said he had previously raised the proposal in a report on digital currency submitted to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and intended to continue pressing for the change.“I will keep speaking on this. The notes of Rs 500, Rs 1,000 and Rs. 2,000 should be scrapped. Only notes of Rs 100 and Rs 200 should be retained,” he was quoted as saying by news agency IANS.Speaking at a press conference, the Telugu Desam Party (TDP) chief argued that reducing the circulation of high-value currency would make it harder to use large amounts of cash for corrupt activities. He also stressed the importance of technology in improving economic opportunities.“If technology is perfect, wealth creation and poverty alleviation are not difficult,” he said.Turning to the recent local body elections in Andhra Pradesh, Naidu said the results showed growing public support for the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA). He also claimed that the alliance had managed to reduce the influence of money power in the polls.According to figures shared by the chief minister, the NDA secured 58.9 per cent of the combined vote in urban local body and Parishad elections. This was 3.6 percentage points higher than the 55.3 per cent it received in the 2024 general elections.The YSR Congress Party's (YSRCP) vote share, meanwhile, fell from 39.81 per cent in 2024 to 33.56 per cent in the local body polls, a decline of 6.25 percentage points. The gap between the two sides stood at 25.34 percentage points, Naidu said.He said the alliance's vote share in urban local body elections was 59.9 per cent, compared with 34.3 per cent for the YSRCP. The NDA also recorded a strike rate of 94 per cent in urban areas.In Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituency (ZPTC) elections, the alliance polled 57.6 per cent of the votes against the YSRCP's 39.7 per cent. The difference between their vote shares was 17.9 percentage points in rural areas.Naidu said the alliance won 575 of the 659 ZPTC seats across Andhra Pradesh, leading in 27 of the state's 28 districts. The YSRCP managed to win more seats than the alliance only in Alluri Sitarama Raju district. It failed to secure even one ZPTC seat in seven districts.In Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituency (MPTC) elections, the NDA won 7,803 of the 9,818 seats. The alliance is also expected to capture around 90 per cent of the Mandal President posts across the state.The chief minister said the alliance's performance was equally strong in urban local bodies. Of the 100 Mayor and Chairperson posts, it won 94, including 12 of the 13 mayoral positions and 82 of the 87 chairperson posts.The TDP secured 70 of these posts, while the Jana Sena Party won 20 and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) four.The alliance also won 3,233 of the 3,941 municipal wards, accounting for 82 per cent of the total. It secured a majority in 95 of the 100 urban local bodies and won every ward in 16 of them.The YSRCP, by comparison, won only four urban local bodies and 558 wards. It failed to win a single ward in 22 urban local bodies, Naidu said.He described the results as a reflection of public backing for good governance, social justice, new leadership and democratic values, adding that the alliance's support had increased significantly since the 2024 general elections.
Article Summary: Andhra Pradesh chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu renewed his call for withdrawing Rs 500 currency notes. NEW DELHI: The accused in an abetment of suicide case who got bail from Supreme Court after spending one year in custody had to stay in jail for another one and a half months as lawyers refused to represent him before the trial court in Baghpat in Uttar Pradesh, which was to pass a formal order to release him and impose terms and conditions for the same.Terming the case "very unusual" and "very disturbing" given that its order had remained unimplemented and the accused was in illegal detention for one and a half months, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and Manmohan directed the jail superintendent to release the man immediately on obtaining a personal bond of Rs 10,000 from him.The accused was arrested in Sept last year and granted bail by SC on Sept 28 this year subject to the terms and conditions that the trial court deemed fit and proper to impose. But the court order could not be enforced as advocates refused to represent him in the trial court, probably because the victim in the case was the child of a local lawyer.Alleging the SC's order was being stonewalled by the local bar association by preventing any lawyer from representing him, the accused again knocked on the door of SC through his advocate Praveen Kumar Jha, seeking its intervention."The deliberate creation of a hostile, terror-filled atmosphere within court precincts to prevent the filing of surety bonds constitutes constructive frustration and subversion of the regular bail order passed by SC.A criminal trial cannot be allowed to continue in a district where the local legal ecosystem, police machinery and local bar have combined to form a singular, hostile front against the accused, thereby creating reasonable apprehension of bias against a fair trial," the petitioner said, pleading transfer of trial in the suicide case out of the state.Besides directing the jail authority to release him, the court sought a response from UP govt on compensation to be paid to the accused for his illegal detention and also directed that the case be brought to the notice of the CJ of Allahabad HC."State is called upon to show cause as to why appropriate compensation should not be awarded to the petitioner for his illegal detention in custody so far, despite the fact that this court ordered release on bail one and a half months back," the bench said.
Article Summary: The accused was arrested in Sept last year and granted bail by SC on Sept 28 this year. BENGALURU/NEW DELHI/T'PURAM: Following in Congress-governed Karnataka's footsteps, the Congress-led govt of Keralam Monday started collecting petrol samples to test whether their ethanol content was more than the prescribed 20%, setting up a likely Centre-state confrontation over E20 fuel.Keralam civil supplies minister Anoop Jacob said officials collected six samples each from nine petrol pumps across Thiruvananthapuram, Ernakulam, Kozhikode and Kannur, in the presence of OMC representatives.PESO-approved bottles and trained officials were used, he said, adding that further rounds of testing would follow and prosecution would be initiated if excess blending was detected.This prompted Union minister of state for petroleum Suresh Gopi to say that states were free to conduct tests but they should avoid political mudslinging. "Let them conduct the tests, whether it is Karnataka or Keralam govt. We have scientific support for it," he said. The minister warned that those creating controversies for political purposes would have to face consequences. Gopi said Centre had permitted 20% blending after assessing scientific feasibility and was implementing the transition gradually.On Monday, Karnataka defended its third-party laboratory findings about ethanol levels of up to 31.2%, rejecting a joint rebuttal by three oil marketing companies - IOCL, BPCL and HPCL.State food and civil supplies minister Rizwan Arshad termed objections raised by the three OMCs "illogical" and accused them of trying to push for a fresh joint survey after recalibrating the ethanol mix.He said state govt would send its findings to Centre, seek changes in testing protocols and demand discounted prices for E20 petrol, stressing that higher ethanol content reduced mileage and raised the effective cost for consumers.Arshad said alleged blending of up to 30% was happening at six terminals where ethanol was mixed with petrol before distribution, not at retail outlets. Karnataka said authorised officials followed prescribed sampling procedures, with labels jointly signed by officials and dealers. After OMC laboratories failed to provide ethanol percentages for the initial 63 samples, the state sent them to NABL-accredited, ISO-certified third-party laboratories.The three OMCs had challenged Karnataka's Oct tests, questioning its sampling and laboratory methodology. They said it did not follow statutory procedures under Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel Control Order, IS 17021 standards or prescribed gas chromatography dilution protocols.
Article Summary: Congress-led govt of Keralam Monday started collecting petrol samples to test whether their ethanol content was more than the prescribed 20%. Article Title: Reds gone, but 'dimagi Naxals' still instigating people: PM Modi

RAIPUR: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday warned that the end of armed Maoist insurgency did not mean the threat had disappeared, alleging that what he called 'Dimagi Naxals' had infiltrated political parties and organisations and were inciting people against the Constitution and democracyContinuing his long-standing tradition of celebrating Diwali with security forces, this time at Karanpur camp in Chhattisgarh's Bastar - once the epicentre of Maoist insurgency and declared free of Naxalism on March 31 this year - he called for identifying and defeating such elements to safeguard the country.Calling it a historic Diwali after nearly five decades of conflict, Modi said this was the first festival of lights when every district in the country was free from Maoist insurgency. "This is the first Diwali after the country has won its decades-long battle against Naxalism and Maoist terror. This is the first Diwali when every district is free from Naxalism," he said, attributing the achievement to the courage, sacrifices and dedication of security forces.Modi asserted that for the first time in 47 years, the CRPF had completed a year without losing a single jawan in operational duty.He described the milestone as a victory of sound policies, political resolve and the bravery and restraint of security personnel. "More than 1,000 jawans sacrificed their lives in Chhattisgarh", he said, recalling the scale of Maoist violence, adding there was a time when more than 230 districts across 20 states were affected.From Bihar and Odisha to Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, vast regions had lived under the shadow of violence, he said. "After sunset, life would come to a standstill. People could not step out of their homes. Naxals had even snatched away people's right to vote," he said.Modi recalled the April 2010 Dantewada massacre in which 76 CRPF personnel were killed and another attack that year in which he said 44 civilians lost their lives. He accused previous govts of treating the insurgency as an incurable problem and abandoning tribal communities to their fate. "Some had accepted that bullets would continue to fly, jawans would die and innocent people would suffer. No country can confront its enemies with an attitude that things will simply continue this way," he said.He credited the change in India's counter-insurgency strategy to the political will demonstrated after his government assumed office in 2014. "We gave our security forces the freedom to take every necessary decision," he said, adding the govt had taken several national security decisions, including measures not widely known to the public, to disrupt funding networks supporting Maoists and separatist organisations.He also alleged that elements within the earlier political and administrative system had provided support to Left-Wing Extremism, which his govt worked to eliminate.Linking the decline in insurgency to development, Modi said Maoists had prevented schools, hospitals, medical facilities, mobile towers and industries from coming up in areas under their influence. Modi said the govt had, therefore, pursued security operations alongside a special development campaign.According to him, more than 15,000km of roads had been constructed in areas affected by Naxalism, along with over 9,500 mobile towers. Nearly 175 Eklavya residential schools had been opened for tribal students, while 50 industrial training institutes and approximately 50 skill development centres were established to improve employment opportunities. He also cited the establishment of thousands of post offices, bank branches and ATMs in previously underserved regions.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security forces in Chhattisgarh's Bastar. Modi said this was the first festival of lights when every district was free from Maoist insurgency. He credited the change in India's counter-insurgency strategy to the political will demonstrated after his government assumed office in 2014.

Article Title: Sonia Gandhi memoir: BJP's Phoolka questions Army timeline, Indira's tears on 1984 riots
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: BJP leader and senior advocate HS Phoolka has challenged Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's account of the 1984 anti-Sikh violence and Operation Blue Star in her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, alleging that some of the details contradict official records and historical documents.He has questioned her account of when the Army was called in following Indira Gandhi's assassination and also disputed her description of the former prime minister's emotional reaction to Operation Blue Star.Speaking to news agency ANI, Phoolka said he had received several calls from media organisations seeking his response to Sonia Gandhi's account that the Army was called in on October 31, 1984, the day then prime minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated."I got several phone calls from media. They said Sonia Gandhi has written that during the 1984 Sikh massacre, the Army was called on 31st October itself. I have purchased the book to read whether this is indeed written in the book. If this is written in the book, it is against the records. It is absolutely false," Phoolka told ANI.Referring to the Misra Commission's findings, Phoolka maintained that the Army was formally called in only on the evening of November 1 and reached the affected areas in significant numbers on November 2.Phoolka also cited the commission's observations on the availability of Army personnel in Delhi during the violence."Misra Commission stated that 5,000 Army personnel were available within Delhi and they were not deployed. Misra Commission stated that had they been deployed, lives of 2,000 Sikhs could have been saved," he said.The Misra Commission found that an additional Army brigade of around 1,600 personnel had reached Delhi from Meerut before midnight on October 31, 1984.However, the Delhi administration delayed formally requisitioning Army assistance. The Army became operational in parts of central and south Delhi by the evening of November 1, while five additional brigades arrived on November 2. The commission observed that deploying around 5,000 available Army personnel on the morning of November 1 could have prevented at least 2,000 deaths."Phoolka also questioned Sonia Gandhi's account of Indira Gandhi's alleged remorse following Operation Blue Star, the military operation carried out at the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar in June 1984.In her memoir, Sonia Gandhi reportedly recounts seeing Indira Gandhi watching a slow-motion recording of the operation's aftermath, with tears in her eyes. She describes the former prime minister's emotional reaction as an expression of pain and regret over the loss of lives during the operation.Disputing this account, Phoolka said it did not appear to be consistent with the historical record. He referred to a fact-finding report prepared by a team led by former Supreme Court judge Justice VM Tarkunde in September 1984, which he said included postmortem reports documenting the aftermath of the military operation."This doesn't seem to be true. In September, Justice Tarkunde's team wrote a fact-finding report on Operation Blue Star. Actual postmortem report was included in the report. The entire team was arrested and the report was banned," he told ANI.Questioning the account of Indira Gandhi's remorse, Phoolka further said, "If you look at the actual facts, you won't find any regrets or tears. It might be crocodile tears."
Article Summary: HS Phoolka has challenged Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's account of 1984 anti- Sikh violence and Operation Blue Star in her memoir. He has questioned her account of when the Army was called in following Indira Gandhi's assassination and also disputed her description of the former prime minister's emotional reaction to the operation. He said the Misra Commission's findings on the availability of Army personnel in Delhi during the violence did not seem to be true.

Article Title: Sonia Gandhi was 'shocked' by Pranab Mukherjee's 'long-held desire' to be PM; his daughter asks why
Article Text:
Sonia on Pranab's PM ambition (PTI file photo)

Sonia on power-sharing with Manmohan Singh

What Sonia wrote about Pranab Mukherjee

Sonia rejects 'back-seat driver' charge

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former Congress chief Sonia Gandhi has recounted how senior party colleague Pranab Mukherjee hinted at his "long-held desire" to become prime minister during a conversation in 2010, leaving her "shocked" with the suggestion that perhaps "it was time for a change at the top. "The account in her newly released memoir, however, has drawn a sharp response from Pranab Mukherjee's daughter Sharmistha, who questioned why her father's ambition could have come as a surprise.Responding to Sonia's memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love", Sharmishtha said there was nothing wrong with a politician aspiring to become prime minister, particularly someone with her father's experience in politics and governance."What's there to get 'shocked' about? Is it a crime to be ambitious, especially when that 'ambition' was supported by decades of experience in politics & governance, hard work & a brilliant mind?" she said.Recalling a conversation with her father, Sharmistha said she had once asked him whether he wanted to become prime minister. He had candidly replied that "any politician worth his salt has this ambition"."My father came from a very humble background. Whatever he achieved in his life was through sheer merit & hard-work.There was no-one to serve him positions, including PM-ship, on a platter due to dynastic entitlements. If a well-deserving person harbours ambition to become Prime Minister, what's wrong in that, unless Sonia ji was 'shocked' by the fact that anyone outside Gandhi-Nehru family could even dare to nurture such an ambition & furthermore dared to 'hint' it to her?" she said.Sharmistha also responded to Sonia's claim that Pranab Mukherjee never made her feel he held her response against him after she changed the subject during their conversation."In this same context, I read that she said she felt 'he never held it against me'. From what I read in his diaries & whatever conversation he had with me, I would like to reassure her that he DID NOT hold it against her or anyone else. He was a pragmatic person with deep understanding. He understood her reasons & insecurities that all human beings are prone to," she said.Also read: Sonia Gandhi memoir: BJP's Phoolka questions Army timeline, Indira's tears on 1984 riots In her memoir, Sonia writes that she was clear about Manmohan Singh being the prime minister and that, while she could offer him her opinions and suggestions as Congress president or disagree with him, it was her duty to defer to him."Further. I was determined not to be under any circumstance the cause of a misunderstanding that could give our opponents occasion to rejoice and weaken our government," she says in the book, which hit the stands on Tuesday.Former Congress chief describes an "unspoken division of responsibility" between the prime minister and herself, which she says worked smoothly: "the government under Dr. Manmohan Singh, and the party under me".She also recounts how the Congress leadership coordinated with the government through a core group that met weekly with the prime minister."A core group met weekly with the prime minister to ensure coordination between the two. Its other members were Pranab Mukherjee, who had been a minister in Indira Gandhi's cabinet in the 70s; the politically insightful Arjun Singh, a former chief minister of Madhya Pradesh; A K Anthony, a former chief minister of Kerala: and Ahmed Patel," she writes."We also met regularly as members of the Strategy Group, set up to discuss issues to be taken up in Parliament. Sometimes Pranab ji, as I always called him, would stay back for a chat," she says.Sonia recalls that Pranab Mukherjee had developed serious differences with then-finance minister P Chidambaram. During one such conversation in 2010, after expressing his frustration, Pranab made the suggestion that "surprised" her."He (Pranab) had developed serious differences with the finance minister P Chidambaram, and on one occasion, in 2010, I think after expressing his frustration, he shocked me with the suggestion that perhaps it was time for a change at the top, which I understood as a hint of his long-held desire to become prime minister," Rajya Sabha member Sonia Gandhi says."I gently changed the subject, and though he may have been disappointed, he never made me feel he held it against me," she adds.Sonia points out that the Congress later nominated Pranab Mukherjee as the UPA's presidential candidate in 2012. He went on to win the election and become the President of India."I often called on him, mostly just to converse with the erudite and knowledgeable politician that he always remained."Addressing allegations that she wielded the real power during the UPA years, when Manmohan Singh served as prime minister from 2004 to 2014, Sonia refers to what she describes as a "rash of stories" in the media. She says some of these accounts were fed by people close to the prime minister."A decade later, a book was published by one of his former aides, reaffirming the malicious and totally false allegations spread all along by my opponents: That I sent for files from the prime minister's office (PMO), interfered with administrative matters, and made key appointments," she says, rejecting the BJP's repeated charge.Sonia says the allegations that she interfered in the functioning of the government were particularly distressing, as she had always been careful to follow established rules."Though I had been the subject of worse accusations over the years, the fabrication that distressed me most was that I was looking into official files something improper for anyone outside the government. I had always been particular about adhering to rules, all the more so during this period," she says.She adds that the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) had issued a statement categorically denying that official files had ever been shown to her.Sonia also cites an interview in which Manmohan Singh's daughter Upinder Singh criticised a book by one of his former aides, describing it as a betrayal of trust and defending the relationship between her father and the Congress leader."Dr. Manmohan Singh's daughter Upinder Singh in an interview called the book 'nothing but a stab in the back. . . a huge betrayal of trust' and 'a mischievous, unethical exercise'. She affirmed that her father's relationship with me was one of 'mutual trust and respect'. However, the opposition and the media looked for every opportunity to spin the narrative that I was the government's 'back-seat driver'," Sonia says.She also gave details on why she turned down PM post after UPA victory in 2004.
Article Summary: Pranab Mukherjee's daughter Sharmistha questions why her father's ambition could have come as a surprise. Sharmishtha says there was nothing wrong with a politician aspiring to become prime minister. Former Congress chief describes an "unspoken division of responsibility" between the prime minister and herself, which she says worked smoothly.

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Tuesday extended the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) restrictions to retired state government officials engaged by state governments in states where assembly elections are scheduled next year.In a letter addressed to the chief secretaries and chief electoral officers of Goa, Manipur, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, the commission said such individuals must maintain political neutrality and refrain from participating in election campaigns."The Commission has in the past, in respect of the conduct of government employees, issued instructions stating that they are not expected to take part in any election campaign or canvassing and should take scrupulous care not to lend their names, official position or authority to assist one individual/political party/group as against another," the letter read."Individuals including retired government officials/officers/employees are attached or engaged or employed or re-employed in various capacities by State/UT governments, for whom there are no specific guidelines or rules relating to their political neutrality and conduct during MCC period," it added.Assembly elections are due in all five states in 2027, with polls expected to be held in February-March. NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi, in her memoir, has said that she has had "practically no real contact" with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, despite his more than 12 years in office. She writes that PM Modi tends to look away and avoid eye contact when they come face-to-face.In her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi said their interactions were largely limited to formal greetings at official gatherings and brief exchanges about her health.Describing their occasional encounters, Sonia said they usually meet at semi-official gatherings, such as the meetings of major political party leaders in the Speaker's chamber at the end of Parliament sessions."It's a very small room, and usually many people are present, but when he comes face-to-face with me, we greet each other with a formal namaste. This is different from the past, when leaders across party divides would treat one another with cordiality. He tends to look away, avoiding eye contact," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi recalled that PM Modi had occasionally enquired about her health after she returned from a hospital stay.He asked, "Theek hain aap?" to which she would reply, "Jee, ab main theek hoon, shukriya.""Apart from such brief exchanges, we have never really conversed, though we've exchanged formal birthday and New Year greetings over the years," she added.Sonia Gandhi said her limited interaction with PM Modi was also set against a wider ideological divide between the two leaders. She described their political rivalry as a contest between contrasting visions of India, rather than a personal feud."We come from different ideological worlds; his idea of this country is vastly different from mine," she wrote.Explaining the difference, Sonia said, "All I learnt about India was assimilated from the members of my family, their lives of service, and their faith in a nation that encompassed a host of races and cultures, languages and faiths, based on principles of liberty and equality for all."On the contrary, she said PM Modi's vision of India was shaped by the RSS and his upbringing."Narendra Modi’s idea of India was constructed by the ideologues of the RSS and the experience of his own growing up. It affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others. In that India, hierarchy, order, and control are central."Sonia said she stood for an India based on inclusiveness, secularism and social justice."He was fighting for his vision of India, and I for mine: an India against hegemony, an India that stands for inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice. It wasn't personal," she wrote.Sonia acknowledged that PM Modi had worked his way up within the RSS from an underprivileged background. However, she questioned the way his humble origins had been portrayed by his public relations team."Modi's origins may not have been as humble as his PR team has made out in marketing his image, but he had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world," she wrote.She also said PM Modi's political journey had been very different from hers. However, she found herself able to understand some of his discomfort with the ruling elite.Recalling her own experiences in Delhi's political circles, Sonia Gandhi said she often felt out of place during discussions in privileged drawing rooms. The views expressed there, she said, were far removed from the realities of ordinary Indians.She added that the suffering and struggle for survival she had witnessed in her constituency and during her travels across the country were unimaginable to this privileged group.Sonia Gandhi also criticised PM Modi's language in Parliament, alleging that he sometimes uses the same coarse language he employs at public rallies."When speaking in Parliament, he at times uses the same coarse language he employs in addressing a public rally. Much of the time he derides the opposition in what can only be termed a tirade," she wrote.She also accused the BJP of repeatedly targeting India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, for establishing the country's democratic and secular foundations."Jawaharlal Nehru, our first prime minister, is a particular target of his party's hostility, for having set our country on a democratic and secular course," Sonia wrote.She further alleged that Sangh Parivar websites were filled with malicious abuse and falsehoods against Nehru.Sonia Gandhi described the BJP's stated goal of a "Congress-free India" as an attempt to eliminate not just the party but also its policies and ideology.She said she believed the hostility towards Congress stemmed from the prime minister's conditioning by the RSS."I tend to believe that this antipathy stems from the conditioning of the prime minister by the RSS. It has inculcated in its cadre a commitment to an exclusionary, hardened version of Hinduism that has been crafted into a political agenda," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi also revisited the 2002 Gujarat riots, which took place when PM Modi was the state's chief minister.Recalling the violence that followed the Godhra train tragedy, she said the Sabarmati Express was returning to Ahmedabad from Ayodhya with Hindu kar sevaks when four coaches caught fire. Fifty-nine pilgrims were killed. She noted that the cause of the fire remained disputed, while the communal violence that followed spread to several parts of Gujarat and claimed predominantly Muslim victims."When I was leader of the opposition in Parliament, I met the victims of many tragedies, and each time I was haunted by the misery I had witnessed," she wrote.She recalled watching television reports of the violence and trying to reach Congress colleagues in Gujarat who were seeking help."We watched the live reports in horror, and tried to get help to our colleagues in Gujarat who were calling us in desperation, but the administration failed to respond," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi said the riots were reported to have been fuelled by a fanatical fringe of the BJP and RSS, including the Bajrang Dal. PM Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat at the time.Sonia also contrasted the RSS's political interpretation of Hinduism with the inclusive understanding of faith she said she had learnt from her mother-in-law.She described this understanding as one that embraced different beliefs and paths, without being tied to a single deity, dogma, prophet or scripture."What I learnt from my mother-in-law is the faith that's been practised for centuries in India by vast numbers of our people -- from stalwarts of the freedom struggle to the poorest in our villages. It embraces diverse beliefs and different paths, adheres to no single deity, dogma, prophet, or scripture, and has included traditions of dissent," she wrote.She added that she had been educated in the principles of ahimsa and dharma as interpreted by Mahatma Gandhi. She also acknowledged the oppression and inequality associated with India's caste system, while pointing out that reformers had used ideas within Hinduism to challenge caste discrimination.
Article Summary: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi has said she has had "practically no real contact" with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. She writes that PM Modi tends to look away and avoid eye contact when they come face-to-face. She also criticised PM Modi's language in Parliament, alleging that he sometimes uses the same coarse language he employs at public rallies.

Article Title: 'Warrants urgent attention': SC flags vehicular pollution in Delhi-NCR, seeks action plan

Vehicles amid Delhi-NCR pollution

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has directed Delhi and three neighbouring states to detail the measures taken to prevent over-age and non-compliant vehicles from entering and operating in the National Capital Region (NCR), citing a sharp rise in vehicular emissions and calling for urgent intervention.The governments of Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan, along with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Delhi Police, have been asked to submit their responses within two weeks, outlining both existing enforcement measures and additional short-term and long-term steps to reduce vehicular pollution.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also sought details of the regulatory framework governing the entry and movement of commercial and private vehicles in Delhi-NCR, particularly those coming from neighbouring states.The authorities have been asked to explain how vehicles that do not meet prescribed emission standards are identified and regulated, including enforcement of Pollution Under Control (PUC) certification requirements.The court observed that Delhi-NCR bears the combined burden of vehicles originating within the region as well as those entering from neighbouring states. It also flagged the substantial volume of commercial and private vehicles adding to the pollution load."There can be little doubt that the issue warrants urgent and immediate intervention," the bench said, a squoted by PTI.The court also sought details of action taken against violations, including the number of vehicles inspected, challaned, denied entry or otherwise proceeded against. It asked the authorities to explain how Delhi and neighbouring states coordinate to regulate inter-state vehicular movement and ensure compliance with emission norms."The respective authorities shall also indicate the specific measures proposed to strengthen the existing enforcement mechanisms, together with a time-bound roadmap for their implementation," the bench said.The states have also been asked to respond to suggestions made by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and the amicus curiae, and spell out any additional measures they propose to take.The directions were issued on November 6 while the court was hearing a suo motu case on air pollution in Delhi-NCR. The bench noted that although stubble-burning incidents had declined substantially across Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan, the data also pointed to a sharp increase in concerns linked to vehicular emissions."While this development is certainly laudable, the same data also brings to the fore a converse and equally pressing concern, namely, the sharp increase in issues attributable to vehicular emissions," it said.The matter will be heard next on November 23.

The governments of Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan, along with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Delhi Police, have been asked to submit their responses within two weeks.

Article Title: 'I'd quake in my seat': Sonia Gandhi recalls Indira Gandhi's temper, early days as bride in memoir
Article Text:
Sonia recalls Indira Gandhi's temper

Indira's love for old photographs, sarees and shawls

NEW DELHI: A staffer made to stand in a corner, a senior Congress leader ordered to face the wall and another person ignored for days. Indira Gandhi had different ways of dealing with those who triggered her “occasional explosions of temper”, Sonia Gandhi writes in her recently released memoir, recalling her early days as a bride in the Nehru-Gandhi family.In her much-anticipated memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, the senior Congress leader offers a glimpse into the temperament of the former prime minister and her mother-in-law, describing how her sudden outbursts could leave even those around her visibly shaken.The 544-page book, published by HarperCollins India, traces the arc of Sonia's life, from her childhood in post-war Italy and marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family to the assassination of her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, and her eventual entry into politics.Also Read| What made Sonia Gandhi turn down PM post after UPA’s 2004 victory? Memoir revisits moment “What I found most alarming was my mother-in-law's occasional explosions of temper. They could freeze the staff into numbness,” she writes.Recalling one such incident, Sonia says a staff member who had repeatedly forgotten to remind Indira of an important appointment was made to stand in a corner of the room as others hurriedly moved around him, visibly embarrassed.In another instance, she came across a “kurta-dhoti-clad individual standing immobile in the corner, staring at the wall”.“I was not yet familiar with who was who in the political pantheon, but the fact that he was within our private space signalled that he must have been a Congress Party senior,” she writes.Sonia recalls spending nearly half an hour with Amie Aunty, a senior member of Indira's staff, before returning to find the man still standing in the same position.Also Read| 'Should've called it Whitewashing, not Belonging': BJP mocks Sonia Gandhi's memoir “When I walked back, the man in white was still stuck to the wall as ordered by my mother-in-law, I learnt later,” she writes.Indira also had another way of expressing her displeasure: Refusing to acknowledge someone altogether. Sonia says there were occasions when the former prime minister would ignore an “offending individual”, leaving them in suspense for days.Her temper could also flare up at the dining table, particularly after a “particularly unpleasant exchange with the opposition” in Parliament. On one such occasion, Indira pushed her thali to the other side of the long dining table in a “fit of anger”.Sonia says these outbursts unsettled her, reminding her of her own father's temper. While she would feel perturbed and shaken, Rajiv and his younger brother Sanjay would sit quietly, waiting for the moment to pass.Rajiv would often reassure her: “Don't let yourself get so scared. She'll be all right in no time.”But such assurances did little to ease her anxiety in the early days of the marriage.“But until I got to know her well, I'd quake in my seat,” Sonia writes.She adds that Indira would usually regret her outbursts and find ways to communicate her remorse to those she had upset. However, she was far less forgiving when she felt a colleague had betrayed her trust.“She'd distance herself and not ever deal with that person again,” Sonia recalls.Beyond her moments of anger, Sonia also describes the domestic routines through which Indira found comfort and relaxation.One of her favourite activities was asking Amie Crishna to bring out boxes of old photographs, which she would then carefully sort by date. At other times, she would take out her sarees and, with the family's help, arrange them according to their provenance, attaching tags to each bundle for easy access.She would also set aside sarees that she had worn only occasionally but which were still in good condition, asking the family to make separate bundles for different relatives.Sonia also writes about Indira's fondness for sarees and old Kashmiri shawls, including several treasured sarees that had belonged to her mother from the pre-khadi period.The frequency of Indira's “tense moments” gradually declined after she became a grandmother.As her grandchildren grew older, they would often be sent to gauge her mood before approaching her. Their presence, Sonia writes, had a calming effect on the former prime minister.“A smile or an innocent question from her grandchildren at once melted her; they helped her to relax and provided much contentedness,” she writes.
Article Summary: Sonia recalls Indira Gandhi's temper in her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love. She recalls how her sudden outbursts could leave even those around her visibly shaken. Sonia also writes about Indira's fondness for sarees and treasured shawls, including several treasured sarees that belonged to her mother.

Article Title: India, US plan joint crackdown on transnational drug cartels, synthetic drug trade

Indian delegation was led by NCB Director General Anurag Garg, while the US side was headed by Debbie Seguin, acting deputy director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy

NEW DELHI: In a push to dismantle transnational narcotics syndicates, top security and policy officials from India and the United States convened in New Delhi for the 2nd India–US Drug Policy Executive Working Group Meeting. The high-level dialogue, hosted by India's Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) on November 2–3, aims to establish a synchronized framework to choke off synthetic drug flows, secure pharmaceutical supply chains, and cut off illicit drug financing across borders.Building on the foundational momentum of their inaugural January 2026 meeting in Washington, D.C., both nations used the two-day session to evaluate evolving trafficking trends and map out rigorous priorities for intelligence sharing, coordinated enforcement actions, precursor control, and demand reduction.The Indian delegation was led by NCB Director General Anurag Garg, while the US side was headed by Debbie Seguin, Acting Deputy Director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP).Opening the discussions, NCB Director General Garg spotlighted the India Vision Roadmap 2026–2029—formulated under the guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.Garg emphasized that India has transitioned to a robust, network-centric enforcement model designed to dismantle the entire illicit ecosystem by targeting kingpins, financiers, chemical suppliers, and logistical facilitators rather than street-level operatives alone.Underscoring the shared threat landscape, ONDCP Director and U.S. Drug Czar Sara Carter stressed that bilateral cooperation is vital to neutralizing transnational cartels that now operate like sophisticated multinational logistics enterprises.Referencing President Trump’s 2026 National Drug Control Strategy, Carter noted that countering these adaptive networks requires an equally targeted international response to secure commercial supply chains against chemical and pharmaceutical diversion.Amplifying the operational impact on the ground, U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor pointed to tangible results delivered by the partnership. Gor stated that both countries are actively choking off illicit precursor chemicals and dismantling cartels through high-trust, rapid law enforcement coordination that safeguards families in both nations.The meeting concluded with a mutual endorsement of key operational and regulatory milestones, including Operation MedMax, Operation WIPE, and India's Voluntary Code of Conduct designed to prevent the diversion of synthetic drug precursors.Both governments reaffirmed their long-term institutional commitment to regular intelligence exchanges, best-practice sharing, and comprehensive demand reduction initiatives.
Article Summary: The high-level dialogue aims to establish a synchronized framework to choke off synthetic drug flows, secure pharmaceutical supply chains, and cut off illicit drug financing across borders. The Indian delegation was led by NCB Director General Anurag Garg, while the US side was headed by Debbie Seguin, Acting Deputy Director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy.

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav made a vow to transform Ayodhya into the “global capital of Sanatan pilgrimage”, pledging transparent temple administration, world-class infrastructure and measures to revive the local economy ahead of his proposed visit to the Ram Temple on December 12.In a lengthy social media post, Yadav also accused the BJP of weakening the bond between Lord Ram and the Nishad community, promised to protect traditional boatmen and warned that those involved in alleged land and circle-rate scams in Ayodhya would face action if his party returned to power.“We are committed to restoring the honour and dignity of the city of Ayodhya,” Akhilesh said, alleging that the number of devotees and pilgrims visiting the temple town had been declining because of the hurt caused by the “theft of the Ram temple”. He said the decline had directly affected the local economy and promised to reverse the trend.“We will both improve and transform it. By introducing transparent administration at Ayodhya’s temple, we will also restore trust. By providing world-class infrastructure, we will make Ayodhya the ‘global capital of Sanatan pilgrimage’,” he said.The SP chief also promised measures to prevent the alleged mistreatment of poor people in the temple town, referring to an incident involving a woman and children collecting oil.“We will create an Ayodhya where no arrogant person can beat a poor woman or a boy or girl collecting oil and humiliate or oppress them,” he said.The SP chief further said that if voted to power, his government would provide oil and ghee through the public distribution system. “Once in government, we will also provide ‘oil and ghee’ in rations to meet the body’s nutritional needs,” he added.He further invoked the association between Lord Ram and Nishadraj, a central figure in the Ramayana tradition, and accused the BJP of attempting to undermine the relationship.“We will promote traditional boating in Ayodhya, so that traditional boatmen benefit from it and the deep bond between Lord Ram and Nishadraj can be restored,” he said.“The BJP wants to break this bond because BJP supremacists never want anyone to remember any scene of Lord Ram and the PDA community embracing one another,” Yadav added.PDA, or Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak (backward classes, Dalits and minorities), is the social coalition that the SP chief has been seeking to consolidate politically.Akhilesh also targeted alleged irregularities in land transactions and the circle rates in Ayodhya, promising scrutiny of land records and action against those responsible. “We will free Ayodhya from outside contractors and scrutinise land records. Outsiders are the ones who have looted Ayodhya,” he said.“No BJP leader or corrupt official involved in the massive circle-rate scam will escape. Their coffers, filled with the proceeds of Ayodhya’s plunder, will be emptied,” he added.The SP chief also called for legal action against people who insult religious deities and prominent figures, saying those who encourage such remarks should also be held accountable. “We will also create a system to ensure that no foul-mouthed person can insult the deities or great figures of any religion, let alone those of Lord Ram or Lord Krishna, or go about freely after doing so,” he said.Yadav further said that those encouraging people who make abusive remarks should also face consequences.“Those who encourage such wicked people who utter abusive words are also complicit in their sin, and they too will be punished appropriately for their involvement in a conspiracy to disrupt social harmony,” he said.Akhilesh's post came amid a political exchange over his proposed December 12 visit to Ayodhya, where he is scheduled to visit the Ram Temple and Hanumangarhi along with his wife, Dimple Yadav. The visit, announced by former SP MLA Pawan Pandey, would be Akhilesh's first to the Ram Temple since its inauguration in January 2024.Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday took an apparent swipe at the SP chief, saying those who had ordered firing on Ram devotees and subjected saints to lathicharge should apologise before visiting the temple.“Those who had neglected and insulted (Ayodhya), who had opened fire on Ram devotees and subjected saints to lathicharge, should certainly come to Ayodhya, but only after apologising. Let them apologise once to Ram devotees and once to the saints. Let them repent for their actions,” Adityanath said at the 10th edition of Deepotsav in Ayodhya, according to PTI.Although he did not name any person or the party, the remarks came hours after the announcement of the proposed temple visit.Read more: 'First apologise to devotees, saints' - UP CM Yogi ahead of Akhilesh Yadav's Ram Temple visit Recalling the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, Adityanath criticised previous governments over the firing on kar sevaks and the alleged neglect of Ayodhya.“There was a time when even uttering the name of Shri Ram in Ayodhya invited lathis and bullets. SRINAGAR: Political parties and civil society groups in Ladakh, apprehensive that the administration might hold Hill Council elections in Dec, on Monday said a winter election schedule would disenfranchise a significant section of the population as nearly 25% of Ladakhis migrate to other parts of the country during the harsh winter season.In Kargil, political parties and religious and social organisations called for a complete shutdown on Tuesday and a candlelight march in the evening, demanding deferment of the elections. Haneefa said he had urged the L-G to reconsider and defer the election schedule, allowing sufficient time for a comprehensive revision of electoral rolls and consultations with all stakeholders.In Leh, Leh Apex Body co-chairman Chering Dorjay Lakrook also urged the administration to postpone the elections until April or May next year, saying constituencies should first be properly delineated to ensure wider public participation.Addressing a news conference alongside members of All Goba Association and Ladakh Buddhist Association members, Lakrook said holding elections after winter would allow more people to participate. Article Title: Adult vaccination remains low; elderly miss cover against flu and shingles
Article Text:
Adult vaccination remains low; elderly miss cover against flu and shingles

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Despite vaccines being available to prevent several infections that can be particularly serious for older people, adult immunisation remains low in India. Influenza, pneumococcal disease and shingles are among the key vaccine-preventable illnesses that pose a risk to older people, but studies point to poor awareness and low uptake of these vaccines. Ahead of World Immunisation Day Tuesday (Nov 10), the findings highlight a significant gap in protection beyond childhood.A multicentre study of 4,998 people aged 60 and above across Chennai, Ballabgarh, Kolkata and Pune found only 1.4% had ever received an influenza vaccine. While just 19.7% had heard of influenza, 35.9% considered vaccines safe and 65.3% were unwilling to pay for vaccination. However, uptake rose to 29.7% when vaccines were offered free of cost at community health camps.Published in 'BMC Public Health' in 2026, the study highlights gaps in awareness, acceptance and access to vaccination among older people.The disease burden is substantial. A separate study published in 'Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses' in April 2026 estimated that influenza among Indians aged 60 and above accounted for 5.3 million respiratory infections, 36,149 hospitalisations and 84,613 deaths in 2021.The researchers found that an annual influenza vaccination programme for older adults could be cost-effective under most of the scenarios assessed."Influenza and pneumococcal infections cause a significant burden among older Indians, accounting for an estimated 1.2 lakh deaths annually. Studies show that influenza vaccination can reduce influenza-associated pneumonia cases by 52% and deaths by 70%, while pneumococcal vaccination can lower hospitalisations by around 27% and deaths by 34%. Yet vaccination coverage among the elderly remains very low," said Dr Neetu Jain, senior consultant, pulmonology, critical care and sleep medicine, PSRI Hospital."Annual flu and pneumococcal vaccination is particularly important for people above 60 and those with COPD, asthma, diabetes or heart disease, as infections can lead to serious complications, including respiratory failure and prolonged hospitalisation," she said.Evidence is also emerging of the economic value of pneumococcal vaccination. A study published in 'Infectious Diseases and Therapy' in Oct 2026 examined the cost-effectiveness of a single dose of the 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) for older adults and people at higher risk. It found that the vaccine could be a cost-effective option compared with existing vaccination approaches.Another infection of concern among older adults is shingles, caused by reactivation of the virus responsible for chicken pox. It can lead to prolonged nerve pain, known as post-herpetic neuralgia. A 2026 paper in 'Indian Journal of Community Medicine' noted the lack of robust population-based data on shingles in India, while citing an estimate of around 45 lakh cases annually. An Indian phase-3 trial of the recombinant zoster vaccine, published in 'Vaccine' in 2025, reported an immune response in 85.7% of participants aged 50 and above."Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines can reduce cases of severe illness, hospitalisation and complications, particularly among older people and those with chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart disease and COPD. Both are non-live vaccines and can be given to elderly people, including those with multiple conditions," said Dr Jatin Ahuja, infectious disease specialist, Apollo Hospitals, Delhi."India also needs to expand adult vaccination to cover shingles. The two-dose recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 50 and above and offers over 90% protection. Tdap or Td boosters, hepatitis B and, where indicated, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines should also be considered," he said.Goa has taken a step towards expanding vaccination beyond childhood through its Life-course Immunisation Policy 2026-2036, launched in Sept. The policy identifies influenza, pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccination among its priorities for elderly, those with chronic illnesses, immunocompromised individuals and healthcare workers.
Article Summary: Influenza, pneumococcal disease and shingles are among the key vaccine- preventable illnesses that pose a risk to older people. Study of 4,998 people aged 60 and above across Chennai, Ballabgarh, Kolkata and Pune found 1.4% had ever received an influenza vaccine.

Article Title: Arpita Singh, celebrated artist who painted real women, dies at 89
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Some critics dubbed her the female M F Husain while others saw echoes of Marc Chagall in her gravity-defying figures. But neither comparison does justice to the distinctive visual language of Arpita Singh, a pioneering post-Independence artist who died in Delhi on Monday at the age of 89.She looked like the friendly aunty next door, but her canvases were another matter. In one famous painting titled Devi Pistol Wali, a many-armed Durga holds a saree pallu, flowers and fruit, while another hand aims a revolver. My Lily Pond’s serenity is shattered by toy soldiers. Across her canvases, the macabre and the mundane, fantasy and reality, share space.When this reporter met her at a Vadehra Art Gallery show some years ago, she had been poring over old maps and architectural drawings, studying the stars and solving crosswords. “I gather things on canvas. When I finish gathering, I start painting,” she said. She could not predict what would end up in a work. “They take a shape of their own.” Her paintings often feel like riddles, asking the viewer to follow her cryptic clues and come to their own answers. She disliked explaining her own art. “There should be a difference between what the viewer sees and what the artist paints.”Asked why her women were often middle-aged, unvarnished and un-eroticised, Singh’s answer was plain: “I don’t decide in advance whether the woman is going to be thin or fat, pretty or ugly.Anyway, glamorous women with hourglass shapes are for film and television. I paint real women.”Roobina Karode, chief curator of the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, put together a retrospective of her work in 2019 to showcase the breadth of her oeuvre. “Her sharp wit, humour and provocations drew inspiration from entangled and chaotic everyday life, amplifying the pressures of contrary forces from a woman’s vantage point,” said Karode.Women were central to her work, but Singh did not treat them as symbols to be decoded. They could be vulnerable and formidable, funny, exhausted and unsettling. The 1990 Devi Pistol Wali caused quite a stir when it was published in a Durga Puja issue of Ananda Bazar Patrika.She was alert to the violence around her, and unwilling to leave it outside the studio. “We live in violent times, and as an artist, I can’t escape that,” she had said. “It stares at me from the front pages of every newspaper and the cover of every news magazine.” Her paintings could connect present-day violence to older histories, while making room for the ordinary objects that marked a life. Sofa sets, potted plants, bouquets and kitchen utensils became, in her words, “my signposts”.Born in Baranagar, Bengal, Singh moved from Calcutta to New Delhi at ten, after her father died. Her school principal persuaded her mother that her daughter’s talent for making charts could benefit from formal art training. Singh earned a diploma in fine arts from Delhi Polytechnic in 1959. In the mid-1960s, she spent four years as a designer at the Weavers’ Service Centre. The interest in textiles, pattern and embroidery shaped her art.In 1985, when Nalini Malani’s plan for a women-only exhibition lost its sponsors, Singh joined Malani, Madhvi Parekh and Nilima Sheikh in pooling money to stage it.In 2010, her 16-panel mural Wish Dream fetched Rs 9.56 crore at Saffronart, then a record price at auction for an Indian woman artist. She received the Padma Bhushan in 2011 and a Lalit Kala Akademi fellowship in 2014. In 2025, London’s Serpentine presented Remembering, her first institutional solo exhibition outside India. She is survived by her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh. Their artist-daughter, Anjum Singh, died of cancer in 2020.
Article Summary: Arpita Singh, a pioneering post-Independence artist, died in Delhi on Monday at the age of 89. In one famous painting titled Devi Pistol Wali, a many-armed Durga holds a saree pallu, flowers and fruit, while another hand aims a revolver. Her paintings often feel like riddles, asking the viewer to follow her cryptic clues.

Article Text:
"Chinas 'R&D' strategy has for decades been built on shortcuts," Rajeev Chandrasekhar said.

China rejects espionage allegations

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Rajeev Chandrasekhar quipped as China has came under scrutiny over the alleged honeytrapping of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, who was reportedly in touch with a Chinese national."Why spend money on R&D when you have an easier, cheaper, faster way to access tech through Honeytrapping ?" the former Rajya Sabha member wrote on X as the developments has redemonstrated the growing national security risks as the US and China compete for dominance in artificial intelligence, with access to sensitive technology emerging as a key battleground.Kerala BJP chief said: "For China the ends justify their means - any means, any way - that’s their way. No global ethics or norms like Trust apply to them. Anyone who has studied Tech history of last 3 decades and Chinas rise will also learn about the “China way”."The leader also highlighted his 6-year-old X post, claiming how "China has harvested (aka stolen) most of its tech from - this Tech proliferation has been helped by people from those countries eithrr [sic] deliberately or stealing."China has rejected allegations that it was involved in an espionage operation targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, calling the claims baseless and a “smearing”."The narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing.", foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a media briefing, as quoted by AFP.The denial comes as Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.US authorities reportedly suspect that she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information about the Nvidia chief and the company.The allegations have also drawn scrutiny to Megaspeed, which buys Nvidia’s AI chips and has been investigated over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to advanced processors restricted from export to China.Huang recently admitted in a message to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues, without naming the woman involved. Nvidia’s board said it had no reason to believe that US national security or the company’s secrets had been compromised, but would examine all available information. Huang has backed the investigation and agreed to cooperate.
Article Summary: BJP leader Rajeev Chandrasekhar quipped as China has came under scrutiny over the alleged honeytrapping of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. "Why spend money on R&D when you have an easier, cheaper, faster way to access tech through Honeytrapping?" he said.
